scenes.title: Key ideas
items: Pool price is the ratio of reserves
When you add ETH to the pool, the pool must remove enough USDC to keep x·y = k.
The more of the pool you move, the further the price moves against you
Arbitrageurs then trade the pool back in line with other markets, and that changes what…
scenes.vo: A constant-product AMM holds two tokens in a pool. It doesn't use an order book. It keeps one rule: reserves of token A times reserves of token B equals k, and k must stay constant (ignoring fees) after every trade. First, Pool price is the ratio of reserves. 100 ETH and 300,000 U.S.D.C. means 1 ETH about 3,000 U.S.D.C. Next, when you add ETH to the pool, the pool must remove enough U.S.D.C. to keep x times y equals k. Then, the more of the pool you move, the further the price moves against you. That gap is price impact. And finally, Arbitrageurs then trade the pool back in line with other markets, and that changes what L.P.s hold. You'll see why that matters in Lesson 2.4.
scenes.cap: A constant-product AMM holds two tokens in a pool. It doesn't use an order book. scenes.title: Worked example: Pool
steps: Effective price ≈ 27,273 ÷ 10 = 2,727 USDC/ETH, which is ~9.1% worse than…
scenes.vo: Let's work an example, step by step. Pool: 100 ETH and 300,000 U.S.D.C., so k equals 30,000,000. Spot price equals 3,000 U.S.D.C./ETH. You swap in 10 ETH (fees ignored): Now try 1 ETH: x' = 101 to y' about 297,030 to you receive about 2,970 U.S.D.C., which is about 1% worse. Ten times the size cost about nine times more in price impact. Size relative to pool depth is what matters, not the size of the trade in dollars. x' = 100 + 10 equals 110. y' = 30,000,000 divided by 110 about 272,727. You receive 300,000 minus 272,727 about 27,273 U.S.D.C.. Effective price about 27,273 divided by 10 equals 2,727 U.S.D.C./ETH, which is about 9.1% worse than spot.
Let's look at the chart: The x times y equals k curve. Take a moment with it. It's everything we've just said, in one picture.

scenes.vo: First, check the price impact the interface shows; if it isn't shown, work it out. Next, Compare with an aggregator quote. Then, set slippage tolerance on purpose (too tight: the swap fails; too loose: you get a bad fill or a sandwich attack, see 2.5). Also, Split large trades or use deeper pools. And finally, Run the before-signing checklist (chain, contract, token, amount, spender).

scenes.q: A pool holds 50 ETH / 150,000 USDC. What is k and the spot price?
scenes.vo: Question one. A pool holds 50 ETH or 150,000 U.S.D.C. What is k and the spot price? [[pause 4]] The answer: k equals 7,500,000; spot equals 3,000 U.S.D.C./ETH.
scenes.cap: Question 1. A pool holds 50 ETH / 150,000 USDC. What is k and the spot price? The answer: k = 7,500,000; spot = 3,000 USDC/ETH.

scenes.q: Why does a 10 ETH swap get a worse average price than a 1 ETH swap in the same pool?
scenes.a: Each unit you add moves the reserve ratio further, so later units in the same trade are priced worse. Price impact grows with trade size relative to reserves.

scenes.q: Who moves the pool price back in line after your trade, and why does that matter to LPs?
scenes.a: Arbitrageurs do. Their trades rebalance what the LP holds, which is where impermanent loss comes from (Lesson 2.4).
